questions.question: What is the primary difference between per-channel and per-block scaling in inference quantization for transformer weight matrices, and why might one be preferred over the other on certain hardware?
questions.choice_A: Per-channel scaling shares one scale across the entire tensor, while per-block scaling uses a unique scale per output row; per-channel is always more accurate.
questions.choice_B: Per-channel scaling uses distinct scales per contiguous group of elements, while per-block uses one scale for the entire tensor; per-block is preferred for accuracy.
questions.choice_C: Per-channel scaling assigns a scale per logical channel (e.g., per output feature), while per-block scaling shares a scale within small blocks (e.g., 32–128 elements), which can map better to SIMD/Tensor Core tiles but slightly reduces accuracy.
questions.choice_D: Per-channel scaling assigns scales per attention head only, while per-block scaling assigns scales per transformer layer; per-block is preferred to reduce calibration cost.

questions.question: SmoothQuant rebalances dynamic range between activations and weights before quantization. Why does this help low-precision inference in large language models?
questions.choice_A: It removes the need for calibration data entirely by learning scales from gradients.
questions.choice_B: It shifts outlier magnitude from dynamically varying activations to static weights, enabling static per-channel weight scaling and easier, faster activation quantization at inference time.
questions.choice_C: It prunes outlier neurons, reducing compute without affecting distribution shift.
questions.choice_D: It enforces symmetric distributions so that zero-points are no longer necessary.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes GPTQ in the context of post-training quantization for LLMs?
questions.choice_A: GPTQ minimizes layerwise quantization error using a second-order (Hessian-informed) approximation on a small calibration set, solving a sequence of local least-squares problems to choose quantized weights.
questions.choice_B: GPTQ performs on-the-fly dynamic quantization during decoding using running activation statistics, with no offline calibration.
questions.choice_C: GPTQ fine-tunes quantized models end-to-end with straight-through estimators to recover accuracy lost by low precision.
questions.choice_D: GPTQ enforces uniform quantization bins learned via K-means to match weight histograms without using gradients or curvature.

questions.question: In grouped/block quantization, how does increasing the block size typically affect the latency–accuracy tradeoff on modern accelerators?
questions.choice_A: Larger blocks increase accuracy and reduce latency because more scales are applied in parallel.
questions.choice_B: Larger blocks reduce both accuracy and memory bandwidth because scales are stored less frequently.
questions.choice_C: Larger blocks increase memory bandwidth demand due to more scales, but improve accuracy.
questions.choice_D: Larger blocks often improve throughput and reduce metadata overhead but can degrade accuracy by forcing more elements to share a single scale.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a common hybrid precision inference scheme for transformer models?
questions.choice_A: All attention computations in 4-bit, all MLP computations in 2-bit, embeddings in 1-bit.
questions.choice_B: Quantize activations to 4-bit while keeping all weights in FP16 to simplify compute schedules.
questions.choice_C: Quantize most weights to 4-bit or 8-bit, keep sensitive operations (e.g., layer normalization, softmax, residual adds) and sometimes outlier channels or small layers (embeddings, final LM head) in FP16/BF16.
questions.choice_D: Keep all tensors in INT8 with per-tensor scaling to minimize dequantization overhead.

questions.question: When evaluating quantized LLMs, why is perplexity an informative but insufficient metric by itself?
questions.choice_A: Perplexity reflects language modeling loss on held-out data, but may not capture robustness to decoding dynamics or compositional reasoning required by downstream tasks.
questions.choice_B: Perplexity measures only the quality of embeddings, not deeper layers.
questions.choice_C: Perplexity directly predicts latency and memory bandwidth requirements.
questions.choice_D: Perplexity is invariant to quantization noise and hence uninformative.

questions.question: Under what conditions does post-training quantization (PTQ) often work well for LLMs without full fine-tuning?
questions.choice_A: When quantizing to 1-bit weights using per-tensor scaling and no calibration data.
questions.choice_B: When activations are quantized symmetrically and weights asymmetrically at 2-bit.
questions.choice_C: When using methods that handle outliers (e.g., per-channel/block scaling, SmoothQuant/AWQ) with a modest calibration set and keeping some sensitive paths in higher precision.
questions.choice_D: Only when the model is retrained end-to-end with quantization-aware training (QAT).

questions.question: Which option is NOT a standard strategy for handling outlier channels during low-precision inference?
questions.choice_A: Per-channel scaling of weights to localize large magnitudes.
questions.choice_B: Moving scale from activations to weights via SmoothQuant-like rescaling.
questions.choice_C: Keeping a small subset of channels in higher precision (hybrid precision).
questions.choice_D: Randomly permuting channel order at inference time to average out outliers.

questions.question: What is a typical tradeoff when quantizing the KV cache in autoregressive decoding to 4-bit with grouped scaling?
questions.choice_A: No memory savings but improved attention quality.
questions.choice_B: Substantial memory and bandwidth savings, with potential degradation in long-context attention accuracy unless using per-head/per-group scales or hybrid precision for sensitive heads.
questions.choice_C: Compute cost increases quadratically with sequence length due to dequantization.
questions.choice_D: KV cache quantization only affects training, not inference.

questions.question: Why is per-tensor scaling often inadequate for activation quantization in transformers?
questions.choice_A: Activation distributions are heavy-tailed with occasional large outliers; a single scale forces most values into a narrow set of bins or triggers severe clipping.
questions.choice_B: Per-tensor scaling requires gradients which are unavailable at inference.
questions.choice_C: Per-tensor scaling introduces nonlinearity that breaks residual connections.
questions.choice_D: Per-tensor scaling prevents use of integer GEMMs on hardware.

questions.question: How does the choice and domain of calibration data influence GPTQ-style PTQ?
questions.choice_A: It does not; GPTQ is data-free.
questions.choice_B: Calibration data only affects activation quantization, not weight quantization.
questions.choice_C: Calibration data determines scale of zero-points but not Hessian estimates.
questions.choice_D: Calibration data affects the empirical loss landscape used to approximate curvature; domain mismatch can produce suboptimal quantization that hurts downstream performance.

questions.question: Which description best matches block quantization of weights on matrix-multiply accelerators?
questions.choice_A: Each weight has its own unique scale and zero-point to maximize accuracy.
questions.choice_B: Contiguous tiles (e.g., 32×1 or 64 elements) share a scale (and optionally zero-point), aligning dequantization with hardware tiles for efficient int GEMMs.
questions.choice_C: Scales are computed per sequence token to adapt to context length.
questions.choice_D: Blocks are defined across layers to share scales and reduce metadata.

questions.question: What is the mathematical intuition behind SmoothQuant’s rescaling step applied to a linear layer output $y = W x$?
questions.choice_A: Replace $W$ with $W + s$ and $x$ with $x - s$ to center the distribution.
questions.choice_B: Apply clipping to $x$ and add noise to $W$ to satisfy the central limit theorem.
questions.choice_C: For a diagonal scaling matrix $S$, rewrite $y = W x = (W S^{-1})(S x)$, choosing per-channel $S$ so that $S x$ has reduced range (easier to quantize) while $W S^{-1}$ absorbs the compensating scale.
questions.choice_D: Normalize $x$ to unit variance and keep $W$ fixed to preserve orthogonality.

questions.question: Which component is commonly kept in higher precision to stabilize quantized transformer inference?
questions.choice_A: Positional embedding lookups only.
questions.choice_B: All matrix multiplications in the MLP blocks.
questions.choice_C: Intermediate attention softmax and layer normalization computations, sometimes the final projection and a few outlier channels.
questions.choice_D: Tokenization and detokenization routines.

questions.question: When measuring the real-world speedup of INT8 or INT4 inference, which consideration is most critical beyond raw MAC throughput claims?
questions.choice_A: The overhead of dequantization/requantization and scale broadcasting, and whether the workload is memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute-bound.
questions.choice_B: Whether the model uses sinusoidal or rotary positional encodings.
questions.choice_C: If the tokenizer is byte-pair or unigram based.
questions.choice_D: The exact value of the learning rate used during pretraining.

questions.question: Why are symmetric quantization schemes commonly used for weights and asymmetric schemes for activations in inference?
questions.choice_A: Weights have inherently positive distributions while activations are zero-mean.
questions.choice_B: Symmetric weight quantization (zero-point at 0) simplifies integer GEMMs and scaling, while activations may be strictly nonnegative or biased, making asymmetric zero-points beneficial.
questions.choice_C: Asymmetric quantization is required for gradients only.
questions.choice_D: Hardware cannot implement symmetric quantization for activations.

questions.question: Why can quantized models show similar perplexity to full-precision models yet underperform on downstream tasks like QA or code generation?
questions.choice_A: Perplexity ignores the vocabulary used by the downstream tasks.
questions.choice_B: Quantized models cannot use attention masks correctly.
questions.choice_C: Small distributional distortions from quantization can interact with decoding heuristics, long-range dependencies, or task-specific prompts, leading to errors not reflected in average token-level loss.
questions.choice_D: Perplexity is computed with different tokenization than downstream tasks.

questions.question: How does GPTQ differ from activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ)-style methods for LLMs?
questions.choice_A: GPTQ uses a second-order objective to minimize reconstruction error with calibration data; AWQ emphasizes preserving large-magnitude/important channels (possibly via clipping or selective higher precision) to protect activation outliers.
questions.choice_B: GPTQ is online and per-token; AWQ is entirely data-free.
questions.choice_C: GPTQ requires full fine-tuning; AWQ does not use scales.
questions.choice_D: They are identical; the names are interchangeable.

questions.question: Dynamic activation quantization during inference can incur latency. How do methods like SmoothQuant mitigate this?
questions.choice_A: By disabling attention so that activations are smaller.
questions.choice_B: By learning zero-points with backpropagation through time.
questions.choice_C: By storing multiple codebooks per token for lookup.
questions.choice_D: By pre-shifting dynamic range from activations into weights offline, enabling static per-channel weight scales and simpler, faster activation quantization paths at runtime.

questions.question: Which statement about grouped scaling granularity is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: Smaller groups always reduce latency and improve accuracy.
questions.choice_B: Larger groups always improve accuracy but hurt latency.
questions.choice_C: Smaller groups generally improve accuracy by tailoring scales more locally but increase metadata and broadcasting overhead; the optimal group size balances accuracy with kernel efficiency.
questions.choice_D: Group size is irrelevant as long as bitwidth is fixed.

questions.question: A practical recipe for hybrid precision in attention blocks that preserves accuracy while saving memory is:
questions.choice_A: INT2 weights and activations everywhere; FP64 only for logits.
questions.choice_B: INT4/INT8 for projection weights (Q, K, V, and output), FP16/BF16 for softmax, layernorm, and sometimes keeping K/V cache at INT8 or mixed precision with per-head scaling.
questions.choice_C: INT1 for embedding tables with per-tensor scaling; FP32 for all MLP layers.
questions.choice_D: All computations in INT8 with per-tensor scales and no exceptions.
